Everything you type here saves by itself. There is no save button and you cannot lose your work. Close the page whenever you like and come back.

What to do

  1. Press Watch, then say whether the cut is good or bad, and add a note if something is wrong.
  2. All three covers get published - YouTube tests them against each other, so you are not choosing one. Only press Report a problem on a cover if something is actually wrong with it (wrong face, text over someone, makes no sense).
  3. Tap any cover to see it full size. To save one, press Save this cover - if your browser does not start the download, right-click that same button and choose Save link as. Either way the file is already named after the video's title, so you never have to rename it. Copy title gives you the matching title text.
  4. If a clip has a Subtitles box, upload that file too. Right-click Save subtitles, choose Save link as, then on YouTube go to Subtitles, ADD LANGUAGE, English, Upload file, With timing. It takes about 20 seconds and it is worth it: our subtitles spell the Iranian names correctly and YouTube's automatic ones do not, and those names are what people search for. Not every clip will have one - only the longer ones to start with.
  5. When you have gone through them all, press Submit all feedback at the bottom. It gives you one block of text - send that to Armin. One message for everything, not one per clip.

Blunt is more useful than polite. If a cut or a cover is bad, say why - "bad" on its own does not tell us what to change.

Guy breaks down the Israeli-Czech business forum in Tel Aviv and why it matters far more than it looks. EU sanctions on Israel need consensus, so a single reliable no vote blocks them. Hungary played that role until Orban lost; Czechia has now taken it over and is deepening ties fast. He also covers the Lebanon agreement, the India partnership, and the two X accounts he rates most for debunking anti-Israel misinformation. Description

There is no neutral news channel in Israel, and Guy walks through the whole landscape to show why. Channel 12 and 13, Ynet, Haaretz, the state broadcaster Kan, i24, Israel Hayom and Channel 14, with where each one actually sits. He also explains why the outlets foreigners read, Jerusalem Post and Times of Israel, are outward-facing and not what Israelis consume, and how the left-right line moved from economics to security after 1967.
